articles.title: Referendum — a non-starter?
articles.content: THE idea of holding areferendumto ascertain public opinion with regard to the creation of more provinces has been floated by some ministers. The prime minister, on the other hand, remains mum on this highly divisive and potentially destabilising subject. No wonder Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari — who heads a major coalition party that also has a major stake in the current system — is vociferously decrying the government for keeping him in the dark and not taking him into confidence about the ‘reset’ or the referendum. But the visible discord among the coalition partners should not be surprising. It is in the dichotomous nature of the hybrid system. The key policies are made outside the political sphere. But the onerous task of implementation is thrown on the shoulders of politicians, often at the cost of their careers and even constituencies. The tradition of setting critical agendas — whether they are related to constitutional experiments, economic shifts, social policies, institutional restructuring, public accountability, internal security, strategic alliances, or war and peace — in secrecy and away from the public glare, is by now quite old. In many instances, even parliament has come into the picture only when the fig leaf of the law or the Constitution is needed to ‘legitimise’ a dubious plan. The ‘decision’ to hold the referendum is also par for the course. The architecture of the reset has never been elucidated. Its proponents are fully aware that a referendum can never substitute for the mandatory constitutional amendment to alter the boundaries of provinces. They also know the tainted history of referendums, which were called to validate the capture of power by dictators. And they may also not deny the fact, as rightly pointed out by BBZ, that the prevailing sociopolitical and security environment in the country is unsuitable for holding a controversial referendum, that too on such a socio-politically explosive issue. Yet, the advocates of referendum seem adamant to carry it through. Why? No one can conjecture the answer with surety because to this day the architecture of the reset has never been elucidated. All that we know is that ‘reset’ is ‘desirable’ for good governance and devolution of power to the lowest strata. But this ‘truism’ is flawed, conceptually and functionally. Conceptually, good governance and devolution being the offshoots of a broader constitutional democratic framework are antithetical to the hybrid system that is extraconstitutional. And functionally, restructuring the entire state fabric requires not only public mandate but an array of democratic tools — an elected parliament, representative governments, independent judiciary, and an apolitical (military and civilian) bureaucracy. Moreover, the increasingly arbitrary, if not authoritarian, mode of governance also makes the conversation on the imperatives of good governance and devolution rather absurd. This raises a pertinent question: are the proponents of ‘reset’ willing to do away with the hybrid system to make way for a legitimate and functional democracy, fulfilling the ‘intended’ objects of reforming governance and empowering local communities? If the hybridity is to stay, then it would be disastrous to ‘reset’ in the name of good governance or devolution, which are the attributes of a functional democracy. Even the reset on the logic of size or demographics is grossly misleading. Size and demography are only two of the many dimensions of an efficient democratic system. There are many countries where large and populated provinces are known for their excellent governance. In fact, the standards of measuring the success or failure of a political system lie in the degree of its constitutional legitimacy, electoral transparency, institutional capacity, and public administration. Therefore, the key questions probing the performance of our political system should be: is the electoral system credible? Is the public mandate respected? Are wealth and resources distributed fairly? Are public functionaries accountable? Is the justice system cheap, fair, and speedy? Is public safety and order a priority? Is the republic peaceable? And, are the citizens’ fundamental rights protected? I would advise the proponents of the ‘reset’ to consider these questions before calling for a controversial referendum that is bound to pit individuals, groups, communities, and even provinces against one another, adding more fault lines to the already much-riven ethno-cultural landscape. The people have seen enough of the ‘yes-no’ binary questions which were framed in referendums to seek personal legitimacy and institutional empowerment for military dictators, rather than reforming governance or empowering the people. Moreover, none of the referendums has earned a mark of credibility or fairness because they were rigged or state-managed. Therefore, they completely lost their utility or worth in the eyes of the people. BBZ is not too off the mark when he warns that holding the referendum is ‘near impossible’ because of the insecure environment in the country. But also, the people, particularly in Sindh, would not accept the results of a referendum, even if it is somehow carried out. Which brings us to the most critical question: what if one or the other of the provinces or a sizeable ethnic community rejected the results of the referendum? This question is crucial because there is hardly any ‘credible’ or ‘neutral’ forum — political, administrative or judicial — to resolve political disputes. Leave aside the grudges of the battered opposition, even BBZ has now cast doubts on the legitimacy of the 27th Amendment that led to the creation of the Federal Constitutional Court. And the FCC is the court of last resort in matters involving politico-constitutional disputes. Given the thick air of mistrust in public institutions, how would a ‘controversial’ referendum act as a stepping stone towards the constitutional ‘reset’? And more so when, among others, the PPP is resolutely opposing the ‘division’ of Sindh. How would the powers that be garner the requisite numbers to amend the Constitution? It would be tragic to pull off a wholesale restructuring of the state employing the carrot-and-stick method. The multiethnic state of 250 million people is too complex, conflict-ridden and even fragile to sustain yet another forced experiment. It requires meaningful dialogue, consensus-making, and democratic reforms to overhaul its political system, not a non-starter referendum or an arbitrary reset.
articles.author: Shahab Usto

articles.title: Love at scale
articles.content: RECENTLY, the second Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children was held in Manila. Ministers and government officials from all over the world came together to assert their commitment to protecting children, and to make concrete pledges to work towards in the next two years. Among the plenary speakers was Dr Nadine Burke Harris, a paediatrician and former surgeon general of the state of California. Her work has been dedicated to making the link between adverse childhood experiences (ACES) — including neglect, violence, poverty and abuse — and long-term impact on adults. Prolonged exposure to toxic stress has a biological response, with negative impacts on health and life potential. These can range from heart disease to obesity and substance misuse, to impact on brain development, with difficulties in learning or self-regulating. On the other hand, the experience of loving and nurturing support can have a buffering effect for children, tempering the effects of their difficult realities. Especially if support is offered early, it can transform a future. That’s why, she argued before global delegations, when it comes to child protection, “infrastructure is love at scale.” The experience of loving and nurturing support can have a buffering effect for children, tempering the effects of difficult realities. What this means is that if done right, child protection systems would represent a continuum of care. Right from prevention to recognising the signs for when an intervention is needed, to appropriate case management, response and essential follow-up. Allocating enough resources to have effective referral pathways, trained personnel and data management — that would be an act of love by those with power over budgets. In Pakistan, the scale of challenges is both vast and daunting. Where do we even start? From children visibly exposed to insecurity on the streets, to those in distant villages quietly experiencing the impacts of climate change on their households, it seems impossible to address all the structural factors behind violence. Chronic economic stress increases the risk of violence within households, as well as of child labour that sends children out without guardrails. Then there is the plethora of departments that need stitching together — health, education, social welfare, law enforcement. Each one has a role that needs to be clearly understood, so that the doctor or teacher seeing a child in suffering knows how to recognise physical and psychological injury, and who should be handling it next. The minister for human rights, speaking before the world, shared the launch of a National Action Plan and strategy for child protection. It is apt that the oversight of this strategy falls under human rights, which must be guaranteed to every child regardless of geography, ethnic or religious identity. However, what is crucial at this point is to acknowledge the need for inter-ministerial and inter-departmental cooperation, for which the MoHR can act as a conduit. The ministry of education and professional training, for instance, has a key role in ensuring that schools are both safe and enabling, and an important point of connection with children and families. It also has a key role in creating a culture of care for children, with educators beginning to disrupt the normalisation of corporal punishment and violence as a tool for discipline. In that sense, the conference was a unique opportunity to really learn from global experiences of navigating bureaucracy and politics, to get to what matters. All this being said, there are limitations to scale. Social services even in the most “developed” contexts can get it wrong, when mechanically applying standards to children or families under stress. Love at scale cannot mean that children are not seen for their individual circumstances, or are separated from families without working through challenges. If anything, love will be made up of the countless tiny acts and steps taken by the frontline workers who come into contact with vulnerable children, the conversations they are able to have, the kindness they show in response. Again, teachers can represent essential allies in a protective ecosystem. Not only do they know individuals, communities and their challenges, but can be reliable sources of support that children see every day. Within a compassionate classroom, they can create trust, joy, and hope for a positive future. The theme for World Children’s Day this year was “My day, my rights, my future.” This is not the first time we have heard words like this; perhaps that is why it is a time of great reckoning in the sphere of human rights and development, with a tragic deficit of resources and trust in the sector. However, what finally needs to be understood is that civil society alone cannot stop all the gaps, even while being able to offer the state both technical support and insights from community work. Manila was an illustration of how it is possible to make space for high-level official dialogue as well as learning from academic research, and ground-level implementation experience incorporating children’s voices. If this time we truly want love at scale, it will take all of us, working to cover the crevices that children can fall through. The writer is CEO of Cities for Children, an organisation that works to protect childhood.
articles.author: Madeeha Ansari

articles.title: Arafat’s legend
articles.content: THAT Yasser Arafat was born in Jerusalem is something a large section of the Zionist media refuses to accept. There was a big debate decades ago about Arafat’s city of birth, and all that the most hawkish in the Zionist media finally accepted was that his mother had delivered him in Jerusalem, where she had gone on a pilgrimage. Palestinians make fun of this logic. The Zionist control of the media shows Arafat’s birth in Cairo, on Aug 24, 1929. However, some official French documents, including a French family record book (livret de famille), used in Arafat’s death certificate in France, said he was born in Jerusalem on Aug 4, 1929. Arafat was denounced as a criminal by those who were themselves involved in crimes and mass murders. On Sept 13, 1993, Yasser Arafat, American President Bill Clinton, Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and other top leaders signed the Oslo Accords (the official name being the Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements). As Dawn’s Washington correspondent I saw, as millions all over the world did on TV, arch-enemies Arafat and Rabin shaking hands on the South Lawn of the White House. His face beaming with triumph and success, Arafat wore his traditional uniform with a cap whose colours and design some people said looked like a Palestinian map. The hardships and the persecution he suffered in life had an effect on his morale. Arafat was dedicated to the liberation of Palestine from Zionist occupation. Once, before going to Europe for a medical check-up, he visited Saladin’s grave in Damascus, saluted it, and said words which his companions said showed tiredness and pessimism. Addressing the grave of the victor of the Battle of Hittin that paved his way for Jerusalem‘s liberation, Arafat said words to the following effect: “Boss! Pray to Allah to send someone who would finish the job.” This “finish the job” phrase was interpreted by the pro-Zionist media as proof of the fact that Arafat had not accepted Israel’s existence. The man behind Arafat’s emergence as a spokesman for the Palestinian cause was himself a legend — Gamal Abdel Nasser. He noticed Arafat’s talents and suggested to young officers in the Egyptian army to be more active in the Palestinian issue. The Palestine Liberation Organisation was formed in 1964, the first leader being Ahmad Shukairi. After several changes in PLO leadership, Arafat finally became its head in 1969 and remained so till his death in 2004. Arafat had a tough life, was close to death several times, survived a plane crash, dodged Israeli bloodhounds, but remained dedicated to his mission — the liberation of Palestine from Zionist occupation. There was variety in his behaviour. It ranged from anger at diplomatic conferences to joviality when needed. Beyond this optimism lay a harsh reality: the Oslo Accords were vague; there was no clear commitment to a two-state solution; conspicuous by its absence was any reference to the fate of Al-Aqsa. Would the holy sanctuary be divided? If so, would any flag other than that of Palestine fly over Jerusalem? A true indication of Arafat’s courage and his ability to withstand pressures and threats — even threats from a person no less than President Bill Clinton — was seen by all the participants at the make-or-break Camp David summit in July 2000. Clinton was the only person in the American team who was not a Jew. The finest account of the diplomatic drama at Camp David is to be seen in The Truth about Camp David by Clayton E. Swisher. One can understand temperatures rising and even seasoned diplomats quarrelling instead of arguing; but, at Camp David, delegates from three countries — America, Israel and Palestine — not only shouted like street bullies but reportedly came to blows. In fact, such was the mood that at one stage Arafat and Clinton got involved in a religious argument, both defending their belief and dogma in a way that was anything but normal. Once Clinton reportedly shouted at Arafat: “It is impossible to ignore the rights of Jews on the Temple Mount! Your cause will be frozen for another year or two.” Finally came the moment when Arafat realised the majority of those present were steeped in ignorance and prejudice and it was time he told them what the issue was and what he was fighting for. He told the delegates: “The Palestinian leader who will give up Jerusalem has not yet been born. I will not betray my people or the trust they have placed in me. Don’t look to me to legitimise the occupation!” The writer is Dawn’s external ombudsman and an author.
articles.author: Muhammad Ali Siddiqi

articles.title: ‘Enemy’ TV
articles.content: FOR months now, the popular Pakistani drama serial Dar-i-Nijaat has been the focus of cultural conversation. Penned by Umera Ahmed, the show sets two generations and competing sets of values against each other. Nearly every aspect of the show has been discussed at length by TV commentators and celebrities. Common people have also got into the act, and one can find innumerable reels and TikToks recording those reactions in the virtual space. The thing about our increasingly virtual world is that borders and boundaries are increasingly difficult to enforce. This is the problem that the increasingly authoritarian government next door that relies in no small way on the demonisation of Pakistan has to confront. Dar-i-Nijaat and the issues that it showcases, it turns out, are also popular in India, particularly among Indian women who have been watching it on YouTube. The furore around the popularity of the show came to a head recently when several “watch parties” were arranged in Bengaluru. One event was planned for this weekend, and guests were going to be treated to a Persian and Arabic dinner after the screening. The invitation also encouraged guests to wear their “best Pakistani ensemble.” Another screening was to be held later at the private theatre of an apartment complex. The host said that she had meant the event to be for her family and friends, who also watch the show. Before long, screenshots of the invitations began to circulate online. Suddenly, outcry developed over the fact that Indians, who are reared on the hatred of Pakistan and Muslims in general, were consuming a show produced by an “enemy nation.” A Pakistani TV show has become a concern for Indian authorities. Suddenly, a Pakistani TV show that has absolutely nothing to do with India had become a concern for Indian authorities. The Bengaluru police got involved and began to “investigate” the two screenings, insinuating that the people watching the show and inviting others to watch were immediately collaborators with the ‘enemy’ nation. Both screenings were cancelled. Other screenings that had already taken place such as one organised in New Delhi also have drawn criticism. An Indian actor named Shoaib Ibrahim who had praised the drama and the cast became the target of horrible online attacks (naturally drawing on his faith). The usual cast of BJP and Hindutva extremists took to TV to spew what has become the typical Indian reaction to anything Pakistani. Their recommendations include a complete ban of anything Pakistani on YouTube, provocations that everyone who likes Pakistani TV dramas should move to Pakistan and even (strangely) that the Pakistani military is somehow involved in the production of these shows, which are meant to inspire Hindu girls to convert to Islam as part of the “love jihad” programme. In Pakistan no one really cares about what these extremists think. This, perhaps, is what galls Indians and particularly BJP hyper-nationalists and Hindu supremacists. Much of Indian cinema is taken up with selling hatred in some form or another. Anti-Pakistan themes are the mainstay of plots and productions. As a drama like Dar-i-Nijaat reveals, Pakistan is concerned with sorting its own issues of traditional values against modernity, new and old ways of relating to the world and to each other, class issues, gender issues and so on. Pakistani dramas try to show the complexity of these issues and because their audience tends largely to be female, they present a perspective that appeals to other women in South Asia and even beyond. The characters of Zaryab, Abu Bakar and Zamil all represent the quandaries of existing in a world where modernity, ambition, aspirations, family bonds and expectations are exerting push and pull factors on the people involved. Indian ultra-nationalists seem to have two contradictory goals. They want to paint Pakistan as the devious enemy that allows them to oppress the rights of Indians in the name of national security. This means that the existence of Pakistan is oddly necessary to their own relevance. On the other hand, they also want to erase the reality of Pakistan from Indian minds. They want to create darr (fear) instead of a doorway (dar) but then also want nijaat (deliverance). In a virtual-dominated world where authoritarian bans cannot completely control the spread of information, this is increasingly impossible. Naturally this frustrates hard-line Indians. More fuel to this fire was added this week with the launch of Pakistan’s first official Netflix production, Jo Bachain Hain Sang Samait Lo. In a move reflective of how far India has fallen, the All-India Cine Workers Union has asked Prime Minister Modi to ban it from Netflix in India. For India, it appears there is no possibility of a Dar-i-Nijaat at all. The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.
articles.author: Rafia Zakaria

articles.title: Loose talk
articles.content: WHERE the Iran war goes, Donald Trump is known for his fantastical pronouncements. Trapped in a conflict of his own making, which he cannot find an honourable exit from, perhaps the US president expresses his frustration through these questionable remarks. Speaking to his troops recently, Mr Trump said hypothetical Iranian atomic weapons could cause a “nuclear holocaust”, which is why Tehran’s nuclear ambitions needed to be curbed. He also termed the Iranian leadership “crazy”. Mr Trump should know that the only undeclared nuclear power in the Middle East is Israel — a state that has bombed and attacked nearly every neighbour. In fact, many far-right figures in the Zionist state, including ministers, have toyed with the idea of using an atomic bomb against Iran. Even the thought of using such weapons is abominable, but when it comes to Israel, it can literally get away with murder. Mr Trump’s recent comments amount to alarmism and creating an imaginary threat from Iran’s non-existent nuclear weapons. He himself said, after attacking Iran in June 2025, that the Islamic Republic’s nuclear facilities had been “obliterated”, while the American intelligence community is of the opinion that Tehran is not building the bomb. Therefore, such scaremongering must be avoided; irresponsible talk such as this only hardens Tehran’s attitude. If anything, the international community must work to ensure that Israel is never able to threaten any of its neighbours, or any other country, with its clandestine nuclear arsenal. Nine months after the US and Israel launched the war on Iran, a stable peace eludes the region. While there are no heavy exchanges of fire, the Strait of Hormuz effectively remains closed and Iranian ports blockaded, while Iranian strikes on pro-US Gulf sheikhdoms continue. As we have said on these pages before, this is an untenable situation for the world, and particularly for this region. The anxiety surrounding the ‘no war, no peace’ status quo must end, and give way to a peaceful solution. The period between now and when the Democrats take control of the US Congress in January is particularly dangerous, as Mr Trump — goaded by Israel and his hawkish domestic advisors — may be tempted to make a rash move against Iran before his powers are clipped. Suffice it to say, another full-blown attack would be devastating, and nearly all regional states have expressed their opposition to more war. Therefore, the US should take the military option off the table, and exclusively work to resolve the crisis through negotiations. Iran must also show flexibility to allow for a negotiated settlement. If the threats and combative rhetoric from Washington and Tel Aviv continue, the possibility of a flare-up and miscalculation is very real.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Prisoners of process
articles.content: IN Pakistan, the assumption of guilt overrides protecting innocence too often. The process becomes the punishment. A Peshawar High Court bench ordered the provincial government and the officials involved to pay Rs10m in compensation to a man who spent a decade in Karachi Central Prison after completing his sentence in a narcotics case without trial. Administrative oversight was the culprit: officials did not move him to KP on a murder charge. The ruling exposes the sad truth of our legal system — already flawed probation and parole processes continue to worsen. The Annual Prisons Data Report 2026, compiled by the National Commission for Human Rights and Justice Project Pakistan, reveals that consideration of protracted incarceration, delays in trials, and the obstacles to procuring bail is past due. It also highlights that, built to hold 68,832 inmates, jails presently function at over 160pc of their capacity. A staggering 110,513 are crammed in foetid conditions; three of every four prisoners, captive to legal limbo, wait for trial. Courts need to mend fractures that paralyse lives. For starters, time limits should be set for both investigations and trial duration. Long-undecided undertrial cases can be heard within prisons, particularly those involving women, children, and people with disabilities. Each adjournment adds more time to a verdict that is yet to come. Bail reforms, assessment of remand decisions, and early legal aid are the need of the hour. The NCHR should be empowered to conduct spot checks and introduce separate prisoner complaint systems. Meanwhile, prison management, in order to ensure proper rehabilitation, must include vocational training and education. Rehabilitation programmes are imperative for those charged with minor offences while people with psychosocial disabilities require treatment, not confinement. The 2022 amendment to the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, which slashed parole and probation for drug offenders, has only led to a rise in imprisonments. The answer to this crisis is political will. Key reforms that centralise the right to liberty, beginning with the enforcement of Draft Prison Rules, 2022, which promise inmate wellbeing, cannot be postponed, together with community service and alternative sentencing. No compensation can return time.
articles.author: Editorial
